narration: This is AIRS-Lite, an AI asset risk lakehouse. It finds the AI running inside a company, scores how risky each tool is, and builds the data platform to control it.

Today, any employee can bring AI into a company in under a minute. A chatbot in the browser. A coding agent that runs shell commands. An MCP plug-in that connects AI to the company database. Or a model running on the laptop. Nobody approved them, and traditional security tools cannot see most of them. This is shadow AI.

It matters. Prompts and uploads are a new way for data to leak. Agents act on their own, with real access. Laws like the EU AI Act now require companies to know and document the AI they use. And companies pay for AI licences that nobody uses.

AIRS-Lite works like airport security for AI. A risk catalog knows every tool. A live event stream watches every action. A real-time engine decides allow, warn or block. Sensitive data is masked, and a tamper-proof log keeps the evidence.

Under the hood, it is a modern data platform. Apache Spark builds the risk catalog in batch. Redpanda carries live events to Apache Flink for real-time decisions. Both engines share Apache Iceberg tables. Apache Airflow orchestrates everything, and Trino and Superset serve the dashboards.
The project has six phases. Two are complete: the platform itself, and the AI risk catalog. Streaming, dashboards, investigation and hardening come next.

In phase zero, we built a thirteen-service platform with Docker Compose, and proved it with a smoke test. Spark, Flink and Airflow all write to the same Iceberg table, and Trino and Superset read every row.

In phase one, we built the AI risk catalog. Every night, an Airflow pipeline pulls real data from five public sources, matches duplicates across them, scores every asset on capability, exposure and governance, keeps the full history of every score, and publishes the changes to Redpanda for the real-time engine.

The proof is in the numbers. Twenty-two thousand real AI assets are scored. Entity matching is measured on every run, with ninety-nine point nine percent precision. Thirty-one unit tests and sixteen data quality checks pass, and every score comes with its reasons.

Real data also exposed real bugs. An MCP server was wrongly merged with Google's AI SDK. Two servers were chained into one asset. Retired assets stayed active. And the first scoring formula marked almost everything as low risk. Each problem was found, fixed, and locked in with a test or a data quality check.

Here is what the catalog says. A package with an open critical advisory is critical. An unapproved coding agent that runs shell commands is high. The same kind of agent, approved and governed, drops to medium.

For the world, this means companies can adopt AI safely instead of blindly. Security teams see and stop risky tools. Compliance teams get audit evidence. Finance cuts wasted licences. And leaders get a clear picture of AI risk.
Next up is phase two: the Flink streaming pipeline that makes real-time decisions. The code and documentation are on GitHub.
